Diversity and prevalence of Bartonella species in small mammals
from Slovakia, Central Europe
Eva Špitalská1 & Lenka Minichová1 & Elena Kocianová1 & Ľudovít Škultéty1 &
Lenka Mahríková2 & Zuzana Hamšíková2 & Mirko Slovák2 & Mária Kazimírová2
Received: 15 June 2017 /Accepted: 15 September 2017
Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany 2017
Abstract Wild-living rodents are important hosts for zoonot-
ic pathogens. Bartonella infections are widespread in rodents;
however, in Slovakia, knowledge on the prevalence of these
bacteria in small mammals is limited. We investigated the
prevalence and diversity of Bartonella species in the spleens
of 640 rodents of six species (Apodemus flavicollis, Apodemus
sylvaticus, Myodes glareolus, Microtus arvalis, Microtus
subterraneus, and Micromys minutus) and in the European
mole (Talpa europaea) from three different habitat types in
south-western and central Slovakia. Overall, the prevalence of
Bartonella spp. in rodents was

of M. arvalis and in T. europaea. However, Bartonella
were not found in the other examined rodents. Molecular anal-
yses of the 16S–23S rRNA intergenic spacer region revealed
the presence of four different Bartonella spp. clusters. We
identified B. taylorii, B. rochalimae, B. elizabethae,
B. grahamii and Bartonella sp. wbs11 in A. flavicollis and
My. glareolus. Bartonella genotypes ascribed to B. taylorii
and B. rochalimae were found in M. arvalis. B. taylorii was
identified in T. europaea. Questing Ixodes ricinus ticks that
were collected at the study sites were not infected with
Bartonella. This study improves our understanding of the
ecoepidemiology of Bartonella spp. in Europe and underlines
the necessity for further research on Bartonella-host-vector
associations and their consequences on animal and human
health in Slovakia.

Introduction
Bartonella, previously known as Grahamella (Birtles et al.
1995), are Gram-negative bacteria of medical and veterinary
importance that belong to the class of alpha-proteobacteria.
They infect the erythrocytes and endothelial cells of mammals
and are adapted to distinct mammalian hosts. Bartonella are
transmitted by ectoparasitic arthropods, although knowledge
of their vectors is not well understood (Regier et al. 2016).
Several blood-feeding arthropods, such as sand flies, human
body lice, fleas, vole ear mites and ticks have been implicated
in Bartonella transmission (Breitschwerdt and Kordick 2000).
Some species of Bartonella (e.g. B. henselae, B. elizabethae,
B. alsatica, B. vinsonii subsp. arupensis, B. bacilliformis,
B. quintana, B. grahamii and B. washoensis) have been asso-
ciated with human diseases with presentations that range from
subclinical and self-limiting infection to severe, life-
threatening disease and have an increased risk of infection in
immunocompromised patients (Breitschwerdt and Kordick
2000; Mogollon-Pasapera et al. 2009; Mosepele et al. 2012;
Regier et al. 2016). Clinical studies have supported the trans-
mission of Bartonella by ticks to humans (Morozova et al.
2005; Billeter et al. 2008, 2012).
Currently, 46 Bartonella species are listed in the Taxonomy

Information (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov). Bartonella phylogeny,
which is based on a genome-wide dataset, has revealed four
lineages. During evolution, these lineages have adapted to a
variety of hosts and developed virulence factors associated
with a diverse set of symptoms (Mullins et al. 2017). In con-
trast to the ancestral lineage 1, lineages 2, 3 and 4 comprise
species isolated from various hosts. While the species of lin-
eage 2 are limited to ruminant hosts and have an overlapping
host range, the diversification of lineages 3 and 4 appear to
result from the adaptation to distinct mammalian hosts (in-
cluding voles, mice, rats, red squirrels, cats, dogs, foxes, rab-
bits and humans). Taxa of lineage 4 comprise a wide range of
divergently adapted species that are frequently found in free-
living host populations. In contrast, the taxa of lineage 3,
except for B. clarridgeiae, were sampled at a low prevalence
(Engel et al. 2011).
Several Bartonella species have been detected in rodents
from various regions worldwide (Gutiérrez et al. 2015).
Among them, B. elizabethae, B. tribocorum, B. grahamii,
B. vinsonii subsp. arupensis and B. washoensis have been
associated with human infections (Daly et al. 1993; Welch
et al. 1999; Kosoy et al. 2003, 2010). These findings underline
the importance of understanding the reservoir competence of
rodents for Bartonella, which is limited in Slovakia.
The yellow-necked mouse, Apodemus flavicollis
(Melchior, 1834), and the bank vole, Myodes glareolus
(Schreber, 1780), belong to predominantly occurring
wild-living rodents in Slovakia. The striped field mouse,
Apodemus agrarius (Pallas, 1771), is found primarily in
the eastern part of the country. These rodents have a small
home range and a relatively short lifespan. Apodemus spp.,
Microtus spp. and My. glareolus are hosts to ectoparasitic
arthropods that play important roles in the maintenance
and circulation of tick-borne microbial agents, such as
Borrelia burgdorferi s.l., Borrelia miyamotoi, Anaplasma/
Ehrlichia, Rickettsia spp., Babesia microti and Candidatus
Neoehrlicha mikurensis (Rizzoli et al. 2014). In Slovakia,
the reservoir competence of wild-living rodents has been
identified for several tick-borne zoonotic pathogens, i.e.
Borrelia afzelii (Hanincová et al. 2003), Cand.
Neoehrlichia mikurensis (Blaňarová et al. 2016;
Hamšíková Svitálková et al. 2016), Babesia microti
(Blaňarová et al. 2016; Hamšíková et al. 2016), and
Borrelia miyamotoi (Hamšíková et al. 2017). However,
the reservoir role of rodents for rickettsiae (Minichová
et al. 2017) and the role of ticks as Bartonella vectors have
not been identified.
Šebek (1960, 1975) was the first to report Bartonella infec-
tions in rodents in former Czechoslovakia. Bartonella sp. be-
longing to lineage 3 was identified by molecular methods in
the spleen of an A. flavicollis female from central Slovakia in
2006 (Špitalská et al. 2008). Furthermore, Karbowiak et al.
(2009) detected Bartonella in erythrocytes in Giemsa-stained
blood smears of A. agrarius from two sites in eastern
Slovakia. Recently, Kraljik et al. (2016) ascribed Bartonella
genotypes in A. agrarius from eastern Slovakia to
B. grahamii, B. taylorii, B. birtlesii, B. clarridgeiae/B.
rochalimae and B. elizabethae/B. tribocorum. Despite these
studies, Bartonella epidemiology and host-vector associations
in Central Europe, including Slovakia, are not well
understood.
The present study analyses the prevalence and diversity of
Bartonella spp. in small mammals from three ecologically
distinct habitats of south-western and central Slovakia. The
presence of Bartonella was examined in rodents as well as
in questing Ixodes ricinus (L., 1758) to determine the role of
ticks in transmission.
Materials and methods
Small mammals and ticks
Small mammals were live-trapped at three sites in Slovakia.
The two sites, Bratislava (202–334 m above sea level, asl),
which represents a suburban forest park with significant an-
thropogenic impact, and Fúgelka (
3 3 6 { \mathrm { - } } 4 3 6 { \mathrm { ~ m } }
asl), which
comprises a non-fragmented deciduous forest, are located in
the Small Carpathian Mountains (south-western Slovakia).
The mountains have densely forested regions that are domi-
nated by sessile oak (Quercus petraea) and European horn-
beam (Carpinus betulus) at lower altitudes and European
beech (Fagus sylvatica) at higher altitudes. The Bratislava
and Fúgelka study sites were described in detail by
Kazimírová et al. (2016). The third site, Prievidza (central
Slovakia; 289 m asl), is near a settlement and represents a
forest-steppe rural area with Carpathian oak-hornbeam forests
(Berthová et al. 2016).
A total of 640 rodents comprising six species (A. flavicollis,
wood mouse Apodemus sylvaticus (L., 1758), My. glareolus,
common vole Microtus arvalis (Pallas, 1778), European pine
vole Microtus subterraneus (de Selys-Longchamps, 1836),
and Eurasian harvest mouse Micromys minutus (Pallas,
1771)) were live-trapped from April–July and September–
October 2012–2014 by Sherman live traps baited with oat
flakes (for details, see Svitálková et al. 2015 and Minichová
et al. 2017). Captured rodents were transported to the labora-
tory, anaesthetized and sacrificed humanely according to the
current laws of the Slovak Republic. A fresh intact corpse of a
European mole Talpa europaea L., 1758 was found in the
suburban forest park in June 2012. Spleen tissue samples were
obtained from each animal and stored in
ethanol for
DNA extraction.
In addition, 5767 questing I. ricinus, including 4795
nymphs and 972 adults, were collected by dragging the veg-
etation in Bratislava and Fúgelka. The ticks were stored in

Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses to test for differences in the prevalence of
bartonellae in rodents between years, seasons and sites were
carried out using Fisher’s exact test with an online calculator
(http://www.socscistatistics.com). A
p

was
considered significant. Ninety-five percent confidence inter-

Diversity of Bartonella in small mammals
Sequence analysis of the 16S–23S rRNA intergenic spacer
region in 153 randomly selected spleen DNA lysates showed
that the Bartonella strains detected among the investigated
rodents, and the European mole belonged to multiple clusters,
including B. taylorii, B. grahamii, B. elizabethae, Bartonella
sp. wbs11 and B. rochalimae. Bartonella spp. in rodents from
Fúgelka and Prievidza belonged to four different clusters and
thus were more diverse than in the small mammals from
Bratislava, where only two clusters (B. taylorii and
B. rochalimae) were detected. The majority of DNA se-
quences were ascribable to B. taylorii (Fig. 1). Sequences
from this study and their GenBank Accession numbers are
given in Table S1.

Discussion
Ectoparasitic arthropods and small mammals play important
roles in the circulation of Bartonella species in Europe (Regier
et al. 2016). Here, we detected the presence of Bartonella in
small mammals from three habitat types in south-western and
central Slovakia, but failed to detect bacteria in questing
I. ricinus ticks.
The role of ticks in the epidemiology of Bartonella is un-
clear (Harrison et al. 2012; Regier et al. 2016; Silaghi et al.
2016), although experimental vector competence studies have
demonstrated the transmission of B. henselae and B. birtlesii
by I. ricinus ticks (Cotté et al. 2008; Reis et al. 2011). Our
findings are supported by studies conducted in Sweden, Great
Britain, Hungary, central Slovakia, Germany, Finland and
Serbia, where Bartonella was not detected in questing ticks
(Billeter et al. 2008; Špitalská et al. 2008; Schorn et al. 2011;
Sormunen et al. 2016; Potkonjak et al. 2016). In contrast, up to
prevalence of Bartonella was detected in questing
I. ricinus from particular sites in Europe (Regier et al. 2016).
Moreover, Bartonella has been detected in engorged ticks
from different hosts. For example, Lipatova et al. (2015) iden-
tified B. grahamii in I. ricinus larvae that were feeding on
small mammals in Lithuania. Recently, Regier et al. (2017)
showed that I. ricinus ticks that were removed from cats were
positive for B. henselae DNA. These results indicate that ticks
become infected by feeding on infected hosts and that
pathogens can survive within ticks, but do not prove that
ticks can transmit the infection to a mammalian host. Thus,
further research is necessary to elucidate the role of ticks in the
transmission of Bartonella spp. Rudolf et al. (2016) also
highlighted the necessity to extend the list of haematophagous
arthropods that are involved in Bartonella transmission, as
they have demonstrated infection of sheep keds (Diptera) with
B. melophagi .

In addition to spatial variations, interspecific differences
and temporal changes in Bartonella prevalence have been
observed in rodents (Wiger 1979; Bajer et al. 2001;
Karbowiak et al. 2005). In our study, the highest total preva-
lence was detected in My. glareolus
and the lowest
was in M. arvalis
, although the values differed between
sites and years (see Table 1). The range of interspecific vari-
ation in Bartonella spp. prevalence may be even greater, as
demonstrated in rodents from Poland
(Karbowiak
et al. 2005) and Norway
(Wiger 1979). These find-
ings suggest that prevalence data may be affected by the den-
sity and dynamics of the rodent populations as well as by the
numbers of examined animals belonging to a particular spe-
cies. Furthermore, seasonal changes in Bartonella prevalence
have also been registered. For example, Pawełczyk et al.
(2004) found that Bartonella infections in the blood of
M. arvalis in Poland were rare in the spring but were common
in summer and autumn. Similar results were obtained in our
study, i.e. a higher prevalence of infection was recorded in
autumn than in spring. This seasonal difference was not de-
tected at the rural site in Prievidza
, which may be due
to the low sample size.
Rodent-associated Bartonella species are genetically di-
verse (Gutiérrez et al. 2015; Regier et al. 2016). The
Bartonella spp. present in the rodents and European mole
investigated in this study were found to belong to multiple
groups, including B. taylorii, B. grahamii, B. elizabethae,
Bartonella sp. wbs11 and B. rochalimae. These species were
clustered into phylogenetic lineages 3 and 4 and were also
confirmed in A. agrarius from eastern Slovakia (Kraljik
et al. 2016). Likewise, Buffet et al. (2012) detected different
Bartonella genotypes that were related to three known species
(B. taylorii, B. grahamii and B. doshiae) and two unidentified
Bartonella species that were associated with rodents in
France. B. taylorii, B. grahamii and B. rochalimae were also
found in rodents in Lithuania (Lipatova et al. 2015) and un-
cultured Bartonella sp., B. grahamii, B. taylorii and
Bartonella sp. N40 were detected in rodents from Germany
(Silaghi et al. 2016).
In this study, the majority of sequences derived from rodent
spleens
were ascribable to B. taylorii. This species
causes infection in animals, although its real pathogenic po-
tential is unknown (Lipatova et al. 2015). We expected to find
B. taylorii and detected it in A. flavicollis, My. glareolus,
M. arvalis and T. europaea. Previously, B. taylorii was
isolated from My. glareolus in the United Kingdom (Bown
et al. 2004) and Siberia (Jiyipong et al. 2014) and was detected
in A. sylvaticus, A. agrarius, A. uralensis (Pallas, 1811),
A. witherbyi (Thomas, 1902), M. minutus, Microtus agrestis
(L., 1761), Microtus spp. and Mus domesticus L., 1758 in
Austria (Schmidt et al. 2014), Lithuania (Lipatova et al.
2015), Sweden (Holmberg et al. 2003), Spain (Gil et al.
2010) and Greece (Tea et al. 2004).
Four sequences derived from A. flavicollis and My.
glareolus in the Fúgelka natural habitat were found to be sim-
ilar to B. grahamii, a causative agent of human renitis
(Kerkhoff et al. 1999). B. grahamii was also isolated from a
human patient in the USA in a region that is endemic to this
pathogen (Eremeeva et al. 2007) and was found to infect dif-
ferent rodent species (A. sylvaticus, A. agrarius, A. uralensis,
A. witherbyi, M. minutus, M. arvalis, M. agrestis and
M. domesticus) (Mogollon-Pasapera et al. 2009; Oksi et al.
2013; Lipatova et al. 2015). Because of its worldwide occur-
rence and its prevalence in Slovakia, B. grahamii may repre-
sent a potential risk for human infection in this country.
We also detected B. elizabethae DNA in A. flavicollis. This
result is surprising because this species is a human pathogen
and has been associated with rats. It was described in 1993 in
the USA, causes endocarditis and is transmitted by fleas
(Mogollon-Pasapera et al. 2009). However, Kraljik et al.
(2016) detected B. elizabethae in wild-living mice
A. agrarius from eastern Slovakia. B. elizabethae was also
cultivated from A. sylvaticus in Georgia (Malania et al.
2016). Although it is unlikely to represent a serious risk for
the local human population, it should be considered a potential
agent of infection to people in contact with rodents.
Fifteen sequences found primarily in A. flavicollis but also
in M. arvalis were clustered into phylogenetic lineage 3 and
showed identity to B. rochalimae, an infectious zoonotic
agent. This species is associated with dogs and foxes (Engel
et al. 2011), although it has been suggested that rodents are
reservoirs for this pathogen (Lin et al. 2008). Our data support
previous identifications of B. rochalimae in My. glareolus in
Lithuania (Lipatova et al. 2015) and France (Buffet et al.
In conclusion, our study provides evidence that a high pro-
portion of rodents from selected sites in south-western and
central Slovakia harbour Bartonella, which can be transmitted
to other hosts including humans. Thus, it is important to con-
tinue investigating Bartonella spp. that circulate in the wildlife
to estimate potential risks for the Slovakian population that
have contact with rodents. Small mammals and humans share
the same environment and thus extensive surveillance should
be performed, especially in areas where humans encounter
small mammals.
